Home Repo

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In South Africa you are 20 times more likely to have your house repossessed than anywhere else in the world.

Summary:
In South Africa more than 150 000 homes were repossessed by banks over the last 20 years. It is 10x to 20x higher than anywhere else in the world. The reason for this is unscrupulous behaviour by banks and also inadequate consumer protection. Elsewhere in the world this does not happen because banks are forced to try and help the consumers before repossessing. In South Africa they are allowed to act immediately upon non-payment and they do so in a big way. Properties are then sold at a fraction of the market price and former home owners are forced to keep on paying. It has ruined tens of thousands of lives and families.

Further information:
In South Africa more than 150 000 homes were repossessed by banks over the last 20 years. It is 10x to 20x higher than anywhere else in the world. The reason for this is unscrupulous behaviour by banks and also inadequate consumer protection. Elsewhere in the world this does not happen because banks are forced to try and help the consumers before repossessing. In South Africa they are allowed to act immediately upon non-payment and they do so in a big way. Properties are then sold at a fraction of the market price and former home owners are forced to keep on paying. It has ruined tens of thousands of lives and families.

The big problem is two-fold:

Banks are allowed to repossess way too fast. Sometime a home owner misses just two payments and the banks repossess. This is not allowed in other countries. There are numerous measures in place to assists defaulting home owners before banks are allowed to repossess.

The properties are then sold in execution by the Sheriff of the Court at a minimal price, sometimes for 1% of the value. The former owners are then still liable for the balance. The Sheriff is not an estate agent and does not care about the prices. In other countries banks are not allowed to sell homes for less that 5-10% of their value. If they do, they have to foot the bill. Sales in execution are also not handles by the Sheriff, but by properly registered estate agents who get the best possible price.

The big thing is: the banks are not forced to do this. They can institute a lot more measures to assist defaulting home owners. However, they do not and go about the business in an unscrupulous and sometimes even fraudulent way.

MORE BACKGROUND

South African laws are in the Stone Age when it comes to home repossessions according to a recent study. SA law specifically prevents repossessed homes being sold at auction with a reserve price in place, which is the opposite of what is required in other countries.

South African laws governing home foreclosure are in the Stone Age compared to other countries, according to a study by Advocate Douglas Shaw, who has argued dozens of cases before the courts on behalf of defaulting borrowers.

It is reckoned that upwards of 10,000 homes are sold at auction every year in South Africa, after the courts have granted judgment against the defaulting home owner. These homes are usually sold for a fraction of their price through sheriffs’ offices around the country.

South African court rules specifically prohibit these homes being sold with a reserve price in place. Other countries require such houses to be sold at market-related prices in a commercially reasonable way. There are instances of houses in SA being sold for as little as R100, prompting accusations of racketeering involving individuals in the banks, sheriffs’ offices and preferred buyers.

Based on an average price of R1,19m for a medium-sized house being sold at 30% below market price, Shaw reckons a typical defaulting borrower loses about R350,000 through the sale in execution process. That amounts to a whopping R3,5bn transfer of value from the have-nots to the haves over the course of single year, and probably vastly understates the true figures. Shaw is now planning to challenge the constitutionality of selling houses at auction without a reserve price, while the National Credit Regulator has announced that it is raising a similar argument against the banks in the High Court.

The banks have argued recently on Talk Radio 702 that they regard the sale in execution process as a last resort, and comply with the rules of the court in sanctioning auctions without a reserve price. Selling at auction in this way allows for a quick sale, but Shaw says this is neither to the benefit of the banks nor the borrower: “The banks would recover a much higher amount if they were to follow the example of other countries by allowing repossessed homes to be sold at close to market value. This would also leave the defaulting borrower with a smaller outstanding loan to the bank.”

As things stand, the banks still pursue the defaulting borrower for any shortfall in receipts from the auction sale.

Legal proceedings start after three months' arrears

Banks typically hand over mortgage loans to their legal departments after three months’ arrears, though it may be some time later before actually applying to the court for judgment against the defaulting borrower, which is necessary before sale in execution order is granted.

By contrast, in Germany the borrower can apply for a temporary suspension of any summons served by a bank on a defaulting borrower if there is a reasonable prospect of repaying the arrears within six months. “This contrasts with SA where banks regularly refuse to withdraw the summons unless the full arrears are paid immediately,” says Shaw.

A German borrower can also apply for suspension of the legal process if the sale in execution may cause hardship contrary to public policy. For example, the medically-certified risk of suicide has been held by German courts as reason to stop legal proceedings.

German borrowers can apply for temporary suspension of the legal process if there is a reasonable prospect of repaying the arrears within six months.

Courts in Scotland will not grant an execution order without first canvassing the debtor’s ability to repay the loan within a reasonable time. This forces the banks to reschedule debts, or at least allow a reasonable time for borrowers to catch up on their arrears.

Belgian law also allows for time extensions to allow debtors to get their affairs in order, the foreclosure proceedings cannot commence unless the judge is satisfied conciliation attempts between debtor and creditor have been made.

In Hungary the law allows for houses to be sold by way of judicial execution, but provides such incentives that the majority of cases involve the bank and the debtor voluntarily agreeing to the lowest price at which the property can be sold, time limits and possibly also the method of calculation of the selling price.

“The average foreclosure period in Europe is about 24 months ranging from around a year in the UK and the Netherlands to about 10 years in Cyprus,” says Shaw.

Unlike SA, in most European countries and states in the US it is essential to establish the market value of the property before sale in execution. In Germany, Poland and Hungary, an evaluation expert is appointed to this task. In Germany, any sale price less than 70% of market value is refused by the authorities. France’s civil code allows the debtor to challenge the reserve price if it is obviously inadequate.

We have been approached by an Advocate, Douglas Shaw, who specializes in fighting the banks. He is willing to speak on camera about the way banks operate and is busy with a PhD on the topic and knows how it works in other countries. He also has a draft document that can serve as the basis for new l;legislation in this regard and has been in contact with the Department of Justice. He is also working on bring a class action lawsuit against the bank for R6 billion which he says they fraudulently took from clients.

We have several case studies:(Douglas has at least 50 willing to speak)

In addition to these case studies we will also have to speak to the Banks involved to get their take on things. We will finalize the case studies in such a way as to get representation of several of the major banks.

Press Release:


Homes Repossessed
Imagine losing your home for an outstanding debt of less than R1000. It might sound outrageous, but South African law makes it possible for banks to foreclose to recoup even the smallest debt. Properties are then sold at a fraction of their market value while homeowners are forced to keep paying. Carte Blanche finds out why South Africans are 20 times more likely to have their homes repossessed than elsewhere in the world.


Script:


Hassan Ibrahim:
…we saw that the house was sold for a thousand rand. For one thousand rand.
V/O:
This family from Lenasia, an area South of Johannesburg lost their family home when Absa auctioned off their million rand house to recover an outstanding debt. It was sold at one, one thousandth of its value.
Hassan:
For a thousand rand, which is not even the value of my garage door on that property.
V/O:
And Hassan is not alone in this. Adrian Pilling is another of thousands of South Africans who have had properties sold for a fraction of their value when banks foreclose to recover debt.
Adrian:
I had a property worth two million rand. The bank sold it for two hundred and five thousand rand.
V/O:
The property on the Vaal Dam was sold in execution because Adrian fell into arrears on the bond. But his troubles were not over. The bank is still after him.
Adrian:
I owed R1,7. It was sold for 205. So take 205 from 1.7. So now I have a debt of one and a half million and I have to find some way of paying it.
V/O:
Douglas Shaw is an advocate from Johannesburg who takes on banks on behalf of clients. He says banks are quite happy to sell properties in execution for next to nothing.
Douglas:
The banks not only do it very badly for very low prices but they do it far more than they do it in other countries.
V/O:
And properties here are more often than not sold for a fraction of their real value.
Douglas:
And so sometimes properties are sold here for 90 percent less than they are worth. For 10 percent of their value. For a thousand rand sometimes. That does not happen in any other country in the world to the degree it happens here.
V/O:
Douglas says that banks here also sell homes in execution with alarming frequency.
Douglas:
And it has happened a hundred thousand times since our constitution came in.

Devi:
So what is the story behind that? Why are they doing it?

Douglas:
Because our law allows them to.
V/O:
Hassan Ibrahim and his family have felt the effect of this law up first-hand. They bought a house in 2007 and developed it further. They were happy there.
Hassan:
Beautiful home. It was our palace.
LINK
But then Hassan lost his job in and they could not make the bond payments anymore. ABSA obtained a court order to sell the house at an auction. Hassan got legal help and staved off the auction. He approached the bank with a proposal.
Hassan:
My situation got better at that point and my daughters were working, and I had money to pay the bank. And we then told them and made them an offer of six thousand rand a month. The bank refused to accept the offer and they said they will proceed to obtain another order to auction this property. They were adamant that were going to sell this property.
Devi:
How were you feeling? How were you sleeping? How were…
Hassan:
We were not sleeping. It was day to day and we know that we are living in a premises where we were so happy living. And now it was going to become someone else’s property.
V/O:
Hassan pursued legal avenues to ward off the sale, including approaching the High Court and Supreme Court of Appeal, but his applications were dismissed.

We asked ABSA about their dealings with Hassan. They replied that prior to obtaining the judgement their “Help-U-Sell programme was offered to this customer and an offer of R600 000 was received …. However Absa were not able to make contact with the customer.”

They also confirmed that Hassan had made repayment proposals but that “these suggestions were not able to fulfil Absa’s minimum forbearance and legal requirements and so were unable to be accepted by the Bank.”

In 2014 the family’s home was sold for a thousand rand. And Hassan is not alone.


Cristinel:
My home, which is valued at R1.5 million was sold in auction because I owed to the bank R927.
V/O:
Cristinel Is/tra/tescu is one of Douglas’s clients. He signed surety for two overdraft facilities with FNB in 2007. When his business went under he could not make the required payments and owed the bank about R35 000 in 2010. The bank obtained a court order to sell his property to recover this debt. Then Cristinel made a last ditch effort.
Cristinel:
I made the payment ninety three percent of the all amount that the bank said I owed them.
V/O:
FNB confirmed to us that the judgement against Cristinel was for about thirty five thousand rand and that prior to the auction he had repaid thirty two thousand five hundred.

However, the payment did not stop the process. Over the next three years Cristinel managed to delay the auction a number of times, but eventually in 2013 his house was sold on auction for 500 000, about a third of its value .
LINK:
Things like this can happen because sales in execution are handled by a Sheriff, and our law prohibits a reserve price to be set. This means a house or property can be sold for any amount.
V/O:
Douglas says that South African banks are very inflexible when it comes to arrears.
Douglas:
For example, in this country we have many clients where we have gone to the bank and said “Look, the guy’s got a job now. He has been in arrears now for a year nut now he’s got a job. Why don’t we just reschedule this amount into the bond and he can pay it off over the next twenty years or whatever.” No they won’t do that. They say “Pay back 100% of the arrears or we are going to sell the house in execution”.
Devi:
So South African banks repo too quickly?
Douglas:
Much too quickly
V/O:
This is what Hassan also experienced when he upped his offer of repayment to the bank.
Hassan:
We were prepared to give them six and half thousand rand and also go back every year, irrespective of the inflation we were still going to give them 10% increment on the amount we were starting with.
V/O:
Again, the bank was not interested at all.

LINK
Christinel says he experienced the same when he asked the banks lawyers to negotiate for terms to pay off the amount he owed.
Cristinel
And I said “Please, make another agreement with me. I am going to pay you but don’t let me out because it will be me, my mother eighty six years old and my son out in the street”.
LINK:
Cristinel says the bank’s lawyers flatly refused his offer.

We asked FNB about this, and the replied that there “were numerous formal payment arrangements with Mr Istratescu… but they have consistently not been met”.
V/O
Though Cristinel’s house was sold on auction in 2013, the sale has not been completed because the bond is actually lodged with ABSA bank. When we visited Cristinel, he had not been informed by the bank that the sale was incomplete.

But selling houses for very little is not illegal, says Douglas. However, he believes it remains highly contentious.
Douglas:
The banks act in an incredibly unethical manner, I believe, in this. Because even though they might be technically able to do it, according to the rules, that does not mean they are not liable. If you act on a statutory authority, you’ve got a law that says you can do something, and you do something that damages a whole lot of people, there is a whole lot of cases about water on this, then you are still liable. So the banks I think should still be liable to pay back the money to these people that they had done this to.
V/O:
In 2004 the Constitutional Court made a landmark ruling about sales in execution in the so-called Japhta case.
Douglas:
It says in paragraph 59 of that judgement that the bank should only sell a property in execution as a last resort. And it also says in the same paragraph that it should use creative alternatives. Right. A last resort does not mean that you say to that person unless you pay a hundred thousand in arrears we are going to take your house. It means they should try everything else first. So if they can reschedule the loan, they must reschedule the loan. That’s what that says.

Devi:
And it is a constitutional court decision.

Douglas:
Constitutional court decision. And that judgement is being ignored by the banks.

Devi:
Why do you think the banks are ignoring that?

Douglas:
Because it does not suit them

Devi:
But that’s not right. It is a Constitutional court ruling.

Douglas:
That is being ignored. Completely.
V/O:
In other countries sales in execution only take place after a valuation has been done.
Douglas:
Once you have a valuation what most countries will then do is to say it’s got to be sold for market price. And there are different ways they do that. Sometimes there is a law that says it’s got to be sold for market price. Other times it is clear in the law that the banks are liable if they don’t sell for market price.
LINK:
In some countries like Australia a panel of estate agents are appointed to sell properties to get the market price, not Sheriffs who have no experience with property.
Douglas:
And then if it doesn’t sell for that price then there is an ordered way of the price dropping. In South Korea and Malaysia the price drops in an ordered way – five percent, ten percent, and every month for three months. And then they usually have a minimum amount that the properties can sell for. In Ghana, and African country, even in Africa there are laws that says eighty five percent.
LINK:
There is a host of other options that countries worldwide employ to help people to keep their homes. In some European countries there is compulsory mediation and rescheduling of loans. And in some countries there is an option to convert to renting the property.
V/O:
To implement a more equitable system in South Africa would not be expensive.
Douglas:
In actual fact we could change the system with one act which would cost hardly any money. To have better system here is just a matter of better laws. It does not cost more to have a good system.
V/O:
But in the meantime Cristinel is living in fear of the upcoming eviction order from the new owner of his house.

Adrian has to fork out a small fortune each month for a property he no longer owns

and the Ibrahim family still mourns the loss of the family home.
Devi:
Why should South Africans care about this story?

Douglas:
Well, a lot of South Africans have a mortgage. This is a threat to them. Every South African with a mortgage, this could happen to you.

Devi:
Especially as we sail into tougher times

Douglas:
Ja. We are heading into tougher times. You do not know what is going to happen. Every South African needs there to be a just and equitable and reasonable system in place and not a system that abuses human rights on a daily basis.

It was sold at one, one thousandth of its value. Hassan: For a thousand rand, which is not even the value of my garage door on that property. V/O: And Hassan is not alone in this. Adrian Pilling is another of thousands of South Africans who have had properties sold for a fraction of their value when banks foreclose to recover debt. Adrian: I had a property worth two million rand. The bank sold it for two hundred and five thousand rand. V/O: The property on the Vaal Dam was sold in execution because Adrian fell into arrears on the bond. But his troubles were not over. The bank is still after him. Adrian: I owed R1,7. It was sold for 205. So take 205 from 1.7. So now I have a debt of one and a half million and I have to find some way of paying it. V/O: Douglas Shaw is an advocate from Johannesburg who takes on banks on behalf of clients. He says banks are quite happy to sell properties in execution for next to nothing. Douglas: The banks not only do it very badly for very low prices but they do it far more than they do it in other countries. V/O: And properties here are more often than not sold for a fraction of their real value. Douglas: And so sometimes properties are sold here for 90 percent less than they are worth. For 10 percent of their value. For a thousand rand sometimes. That does not happen in any other country in the world to the degree it happens here. V/O: Douglas says that banks here also sell homes in execution with alarming frequency. Douglas: And it has happened a hundred thousand times since our constitution came in. Devi: So what is the story behind that? Why are they doing it? Douglas: Because our law allows them to. V/O: Hassan Ibrahim and his family have felt the effect of this law up first-hand. They bought a house in 2007 and developed it further. They were happy there. Hassan: Beautiful home. It was our palace. LINK But then Hassan lost his job in and they could not make the bond payments anymore. ABSA obtained a court order to sell the house at an auction. Hassan got legal help and staved off the auction. He approached the bank with a proposal. Hassan: My situation got better at that point and my daughters were working, and I had money to pay the bank. And we then told them and made them an offer of six thousand rand a month. The bank refused to accept the offer and they said they will proceed to obtain another order to auction this property. They were adamant that were going to sell this property. Devi: How were you feeling? How were you sleeping? How were… Hassan: We were not sleeping. It was day to day and we know that we are living in a premises where we were so happy living. And now it was going to become someone else’s property. V/O: Hassan pursued legal avenues to ward off the sale, including approaching the High Court and Supreme Court of Appeal, but his applications were dismissed. We asked ABSA about their dealings with Hassan. They replied that prior to obtaining the judgement their “Help-U-Sell programme was offered to this customer and an offer of R600 000 was received …. However Absa were not able to make contact with the customer.” They also confirmed that Hassan had made repayment proposals but that “these suggestions were not able to fulfil Absa’s minimum forbearance and legal requirements and so were unable to be accepted by the Bank.” In 2014 the family’s home was sold for a thousand rand. And Hassan is not alone. Cristinel: My home, which is valued at R1.5 million was sold in auction because I owed to the bank R927. V/O: Cristinel Is/tra/tescu is one of Douglas’s clients. He signed surety for two overdraft facilities with FNB in 2007. When his business went under he could not make the required payments and owed the bank about R35 000 in 2010. The bank obtained a court order to sell his property to recover this debt. Then Cristinel made a last ditch effort. Cristinel: I made the payment ninety three percent of the all amount that the bank said I owed them. V/O: FNB confirmed to us that the judgement against Cristinel was for about thirty five thousand rand and that prior to the auction he had repaid thirty two thousand five hundred. However, the payment did not stop the process. Over the next three years Cristinel managed to delay the auction a number of times, but eventually in 2013 his house was sold on auction for 500 000, about a third of its value . LINK: Things like this can happen because sales in execution are handled by a Sheriff, and our law prohibits a reserve price to be set. This means a house or property can be sold for any amount. V/O: Douglas says that South African banks are very inflexible when it comes to arrears. Douglas: For example, in this country we have many clients where we have gone to the bank and said “Look, the guy’s got a job now. He has been in arrears now for a year nut now he’s got a job. Why don’t we just reschedule this amount into the bond and he can pay it off over the next twenty years or whatever.” No they won’t do that. They say “Pay back 100% of the arrears or we are going to sell the house in execution”. Devi: So South African banks repo too quickly? Douglas: Much too quickly V/O: This is what Hassan also experienced when he upped his offer of repayment to the bank. Hassan: We were prepared to give them six and half thousand rand and also go back every year, irrespective of the inflation we were still going to give them 10% increment on the amount we were starting with. V/O: Again, the bank was not interested at all. LINK Christinel says he experienced the same when he asked the banks lawyers to negotiate for terms to pay off the amount he owed. Cristinel And I said “Please, make another agreement with me. I am going to pay you but don’t let me out because it will be me, my mother eighty six years old and my son out in the street”. LINK: Cristinel says the bank’s lawyers flatly refused his offer. We asked FNB about this, and the replied that there “were numerous formal payment arrangements with Mr Istratescu… but they have consistently not been met”. V/O Though Cristinel’s house was sold on auction in 2013, the sale has not been completed because the bond is actually lodged with ABSA bank. When we visited Cristinel, he had not been informed by the bank that the sale was incomplete. But selling houses for very little is not illegal, says Douglas. However, he believes it remains highly contentious. Douglas: The banks act in an incredibly unethical manner, I believe, in this. Because even though they might be technically able to do it, according to the rules, that does not mean they are not liable. If you act on a statutory authority, you’ve got a law that says you can do something, and you do something that damages a whole lot of people, there is a whole lot of cases about water on this, then you are still liable. So the banks I think should still be liable to pay back the money to these people that they had done this to. V/O: In 2004 the Constitutional Court made a landmark ruling about sales in execution in the so-called Japhta case. Douglas: It says in paragraph 59 of that judgement that the bank should only sell a property in execution as a last resort. And it also says in the same paragraph that it should use creative alternatives. Right. A last resort does not mean that you say to that person unless you pay a hundred thousand in arrears we are going to take your house. It means they should try everything else first. So if they can reschedule the loan, they must reschedule the loan. That’s what that says. Devi: And it is a constitutional court decision. Douglas: Constitutional court decision. And that judgement is being ignored by the banks. Devi: Why do you think the banks are ignoring that? Douglas: Because it does not suit them Devi: But that’s not right. It is a Constitutional court ruling. Douglas: That is being ignored. Completely. V/O: In other countries sales in execution only take place after a valuation has been done. Douglas: Once you have a valuation what most countries will then do is to say it’s got to be sold for market price. And there are different ways they do that. Sometimes there is a law that says it’s got to be sold for market price. Other times it is clear in the law that the banks are liable if they don’t sell for market price. LINK: In some countries like Australia a panel of estate agents are appointed to sell properties to get the market price, not Sheriffs who have no experience with property. Douglas: And then if it doesn’t sell for that price then there is an ordered way of the price dropping. In South Korea and Malaysia the price drops in an ordered way – five percent, ten percent, and every month for three months. And then they usually have a minimum amount that the properties can sell for. In Ghana, and African country, even in Africa there are laws that says eighty five percent. LINK: There is a host of other options that countries worldwide employ to help people to keep their homes. In some European countries there is compulsory mediation and rescheduling of loans. And in some countries there is an option to convert to renting the property. V/O: To implement a more equitable system in South Africa would not be expensive. Douglas: In actual fact we could change the system with one act which would cost hardly any money. To have better system here is just a matter of better laws. It does not cost more to have a good system. V/O: But in the meantime Cristinel is living in fear of the upcoming eviction order from the new owner of his house. Adrian has to fork out a small fortune each month for a property he no longer owns and the Ibrahim family still mourns the loss of the family home. Devi: Why should South Africans care about this story? Douglas: Well, a lot of South Africans have a mortgage. This is a threat to them. Every South African with a mortgage, this could happen to you. Devi: Especially as we sail into tougher times Douglas: Ja. We are heading into tougher times. You do not know what is going to happen. Every South African needs there to be a just and equitable and reasonable system in place and not a system that abuses human rights on a daily basis. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In South Africa you are 20 times more likely to have your house repossessed than anywhere else in the world.
metadata.Summary: In South Africa more than 150 000 homes were repossessed by banks over the last 20 years. It is 10x to 20x higher than anywhere else in the world. The reason for this is unscrupulous behaviour by banks and also inadequate consumer protection. Elsewhere in the world this does not happen because banks are forced to try and help the consumers before repossessing. In South Africa they are allowed to act immediately upon non-payment and they do so in a big way. Properties are then sold at a fraction of the market price and former home owners are forced to keep on paying. It has ruined tens of thousands of lives and families.
metadata.Further information: In South Africa more than 150 000 homes were repossessed by banks over the last 20 years. It is 10x to 20x higher than anywhere else in the world. The reason for this is unscrupulous behaviour by banks and also inadequate consumer protection. Elsewhere in the world this does not happen because banks are forced to try and help the consumers before repossessing. In South Africa they are allowed to act immediately upon non-payment and they do so in a big way. Properties are then sold at a fraction of the market price and former home owners are forced to keep on paying. It has ruined tens of thousands of lives and families. The big problem is two-fold: Banks are allowed to repossess way too fast. Sometime a home owner misses just two payments and the banks repossess. This is not allowed in other countries. There are numerous measures in place to assists defaulting home owners before banks are allowed to repossess. The properties are then sold in execution by the Sheriff of the Court at a minimal price, sometimes for 1% of the value. The former owners are then still liable for the balance. The Sheriff is not an estate agent and does not care about the prices. In other countries banks are not allowed to sell homes for less that 5-10% of their value. If they do, they have to foot the bill. Sales in execution are also not handles by the Sheriff, but by properly registered estate agents who get the best possible price. The big thing is: the banks are not forced to do this. They can institute a lot more measures to assist defaulting home owners. However, they do not and go about the business in an unscrupulous and sometimes even fraudulent way. MORE BACKGROUND South African laws are in the Stone Age when it comes to home repossessions according to a recent study. SA law specifically prevents repossessed homes being sold at auction with a reserve price in place, which is the opposite of what is required in other countries. South African laws governing home foreclosure are in the Stone Age compared to other countries, according to a study by Advocate Douglas Shaw, who has argued dozens of cases before the courts on behalf of defaulting borrowers. It is reckoned that upwards of 10,000 homes are sold at auction every year in South Africa, after the courts have granted judgment against the defaulting home owner. These homes are usually sold for a fraction of their price through sheriffs’ offices around the country. South African court rules specifically prohibit these homes being sold with a reserve price in place. Other countries require such houses to be sold at market-related prices in a commercially reasonable way. There are instances of houses in SA being sold for as little as R100, prompting accusations of racketeering involving individuals in the banks, sheriffs’ offices and preferred buyers. Based on an average price of R1,19m for a medium-sized house being sold at 30% below market price, Shaw reckons a typical defaulting borrower loses about R350,000 through the sale in execution process. That amounts to a whopping R3,5bn transfer of value from the have-nots to the haves over the course of single year, and probably vastly understates the true figures. Shaw is now planning to challenge the constitutionality of selling houses at auction without a reserve price, while the National Credit Regulator has announced that it is raising a similar argument against the banks in the High Court. The banks have argued recently on Talk Radio 702 that they regard the sale in execution process as a last resort, and comply with the rules of the court in sanctioning auctions without a reserve price. Selling at auction in this way allows for a quick sale, but Shaw says this is neither to the benefit of the banks nor the borrower: “The banks would recover a much higher amount if they were to follow the example of other countries by allowing repossessed homes to be sold at close to market value. This would also leave the defaulting borrower with a smaller outstanding loan to the bank.” As things stand, the banks still pursue the defaulting borrower for any shortfall in receipts from the auction sale. Legal proceedings start after three months' arrears Banks typically hand over mortgage loans to their legal departments after three months’ arrears, though it may be some time later before actually applying to the court for judgment against the defaulting borrower, which is necessary before sale in execution order is granted. By contrast, in Germany the borrower can apply for a temporary suspension of any summons served by a bank on a defaulting borrower if there is a reasonable prospect of repaying the arrears within six months. “This contrasts with SA where banks regularly refuse to withdraw the summons unless the full arrears are paid immediately,” says Shaw. A German borrower can also apply for suspension of the legal process if the sale in execution may cause hardship contrary to public policy. For example, the medically-certified risk of suicide has been held by German courts as reason to stop legal proceedings. German borrowers can apply for temporary suspension of the legal process if there is a reasonable prospect of repaying the arrears within six months. Courts in Scotland will not grant an execution order without first canvassing the debtor’s ability to repay the loan within a reasonable time. This forces the banks to reschedule debts, or at least allow a reasonable time for borrowers to catch up on their arrears. Belgian law also allows for time extensions to allow debtors to get their affairs in order, the foreclosure proceedings cannot commence unless the judge is satisfied conciliation attempts between debtor and creditor have been made. In Hungary the law allows for houses to be sold by way of judicial execution, but provides such incentives that the majority of cases involve the bank and the debtor voluntarily agreeing to the lowest price at which the property can be sold, time limits and possibly also the method of calculation of the selling price. “The average foreclosure period in Europe is about 24 months ranging from around a year in the UK and the Netherlands to about 10 years in Cyprus,” says Shaw. Unlike SA, in most European countries and states in the US it is essential to establish the market value of the property before sale in execution. In Germany, Poland and Hungary, an evaluation expert is appointed to this task. In Germany, any sale price less than 70% of market value is refused by the authorities. France’s civil code allows the debtor to challenge the reserve price if it is obviously inadequate. We have been approached by an Advocate, Douglas Shaw, who specializes in fighting the banks. He is willing to speak on camera about the way banks operate and is busy with a PhD on the topic and knows how it works in other countries. He also has a draft document that can serve as the basis for new l;legislation in this regard and has been in contact with the Department of Justice. He is also working on bring a class action lawsuit against the bank for R6 billion which he says they fraudulently took from clients. We have several case studies:(Douglas has at least 50 willing to speak) In addition to these case studies we will also have to speak to the Banks involved to get their take on things. We will finalize the case studies in such a way as to get representation of several of the major banks.
